interior-point.caption: Both lines count quantum cycles for a single Newton system inside a quantum interior point method for linear programming, against the precision to which the solution has to be read back out as ordinary numbers. Orange is one run of the quantum linear solver, the part a faster algorithm could shrink, and it sits below the classical solve at every precision; navy is what actually has to be paid, because recovering a solution of dimension d costs on the order of d divided by the precision squared repetitions of that entire run, which lifts the total far above the classical line. The values were computed here from the paper's equation (10) on a generated linear program, and they make the paper's own point: this readout cost is untouched by any improvement to the solver or to the interior point method wrapped around it.

interior-point.method: Computed on this machine, not copied from the paper: equation (10) of arXiv:2604.24362 evaluated by the local reimplementation on the first Newton system of a generated linear program with 180 variables and 60 constraints, whose modified normal equation system came out with dimension 240, sparsity 122 and condition number 18.4, swept over the readout precision from 0.1 down to one millionth; the reference line is the same instance solved classically here in 54 ms, converted to cycles at the paper's 800 ps figure for one entangling gate. The instance generator is seeded from the values given, so the same request reproduces the same instance and the same numbers.
interior-point.paper: Practical lower bounds for hybrid quantum interior point methods in linear programming
interior-point.title: The readout, not the solver, sets the cost of a quantum interior point step

knapsack.caption: Elapsed processor cycles needed to solve knapsack instances of growing size, for the classical state of the art solver COMBO and for the search built on the quantum tree generator, on the hard instance group. The quantum curve rises far more slowly, so it passes below COMBO at about 100 items and is more than a factor of ten cheaper at 600 items: the point is the slope, not any single value. Numbers are read off the published cycle count figure, which is figure 6.2 of the thesis; the quantum values in this group are estimates obtained from the dequantised classical tree generator rather than full simulation, and COMBO returns a proven optimum while the quantum search returns the optimum only with some probability. This tool costs the tree generator circuit itself and takes the amplification schedule as given, so it does not reproduce these end to end totals.

knapsack-variants.caption: Each line is the number of logical gates needed to build the quantum tree generator, the circuit that puts every feasible packing into superposition, for one of the three knapsack problems as the number of items grows. The plain problem stays close to linear, adding more kinds of weight limit multiplies the cost by roughly the number of limits, and paying a bonus for every pair of chosen items turns the growth quadratic: at 320 items the quadratic circuit costs about 37 times the plain one. The values are ours rather than the authors' own, because the paper states these two circuits structurally and its simulator is not published, so the counts were computed by our reimplementation on generated instances.

linear-solvers.caption: Median number of oracle query calls made by four quantum linear solvers on the three data sets of the paper: random instances built to satisfy the assumptions of functional quantum linear solvers, linear systems taken from simplex iterations on MIPLIB, and discretised Poisson equations. The vertical axis is logarithmic and spans nineteen decades, which is what it takes to hold HHL and the rest in one picture: HHL costs between eight and eleven orders of magnitude more queries than the cheapest of the other three on every data set. On the random instances the method based on the quantum singular value transformation is the cheapest by about two orders of magnitude, while on the two structured data sets the Chebyshev method comes out slightly ahead of it, so the advantage of that method is clearest where the assumptions hold exactly. The values are medians computed here from the query counts published in that repository, not from our own library, which follows the printed lemmas in three places where the repository does not: the round count of amplitude amplification, the logarithm base in the j0 bound, and the logarithm base and crossover test in the Hamiltonian simulation cost. Our own numbers for these four solvers therefore differ from the ones plotted.

max-flow.caption: Each line is the expected cost of finding every vertex of one breadth first search layer, as the size of the list being searched grows: navy for the quantum search, counted in gates, orange for a classical scan that looks at each vertex once. The three navy lines are for layers holding 1, 10 and 100 of the vertices being sought, the list itself being the whole vertex set of the graph. Quantum stays above classical across the whole range the paper's benchmark instances cover, 50 to about 300,000 vertices, by about 16 times at a list of 100 and about 1,500 times at 300,000 when a single vertex is sought, which is why the paper concludes that quantum breadth first search cannot beat the classical one here; the values were computed on this machine from the paper's own Lemmas 1 and 2 with the hybrid benchmarking library, not measured on the paper's instances.

simplex.caption: The vertical axis is the time a single quantum gate would have to take, on a logarithmic scale spanning fifteen powers of ten. To beat one iteration of the classical simplex method on the benchmark instances, the quantum simplex would need a gate time between 10 to the minus 18 and 10 to the minus 21 seconds, while the fastest isolated gate operation ever measured is 6.5 nanoseconds and control electronics in the 1 to 10 GHz range put a floor near 0.1 nanoseconds. All values are taken from section 4.6 of the thesis, results R1 and R2, which accompany figures 4.4 to 4.6.
